sections.h2: Which Tompkinsville offices collect and assess Monroe County tax?
sections.html:
Courthouse suites at 200 North Main Street in Tompkinsville hold most of the tax offices. The PVA values the homes, the sheriff takes in the payment, and the county clerk looks after delinquent bills and liens. The county attorney, in a separate office on North Main Street, arranges payment plans.

This is the Kentucky Monroe County, in the Eastern Pennyroyal Plateau.

sections.h2: What is Monroe County like beyond the courthouse?
sections.html:
Monroe spreads across about 329 square miles of land along the Tennessee border. Formed in 1820, it carries the name of President James Monroe, and its seat honors his vice president, Daniel Tompkins. Wikipedia says no other county named for a president has a seat named for that president's vice president. Fountain Run and Gamaliel are the other cities. Neighbors are Barren, Metcalfe, Cumberland and Allen counties, plus Clay and Macon counties in Tennessee.

The county website describes the Upper Cumberland hills, the Cumberland River and the headwaters of the Barren River. History is visible on the ground: the Old Mulkey Meetinghouse State Historic Site holds the oldest log meetinghouse in Kentucky, built in 1804, on a 20 acre park. Confederate raiders under John Hunt Morgan attacked a Union garrison here on July 9, 1862, and captured 30 soldiers, per Wikipedia.

Wikipedia adds that Monroe stayed a dry county until voters approved alcohol sales on November 7, 2023.

sections.h2: Is the Monroe County housing market growing?
sections.html:
Monroe is the only one of these four counties to shrink since 2020. The 2020 count of 11,338 topped the 10,963 recorded in 2010, but the mid-2025 estimate of 11,191 is 1.3 percent lower. Housing units number 5,300.

Five year survey results:

  • The share of owner lived homes is 70.9 percent, the smallest of the four counties, which leaves more room for rentals.
  • Monthly owner costs are $1,056 with a mortgage and $397 without one.
  • Broadband is subscribed to by 83.9 percent of households.
  • Workers average 28.4 minutes to reach a job.
  • Jobs counted in 2023 came to 2,649, which is 1.9 percent below 2022.
  • Per capita income is $27,296, and 88.7 percent of households have a computer.

sections.h2: Which Monroe County offices should you call or visit?
sections.html:
The county officials page gives these courthouse suites, all in Tompkinsville, KY 42167.

  • Sheriff: tax collection. 200 North Main Street, Suite E, phone (270) 487-6622.
  • PVA: assessments and exemptions. 200 North Main Street, Suite A, phone (270) 487-6401.
  • County Clerk: delinquent bills and liens. 200 North Main Street, Suite D, phone (270) 487-5471.
  • County Attorney: 215 North Main Street, phone (270) 487-6303.

Before paying anyone, learn from the clerk whether your certificate has been sold, because a buyer can attach costs of its own.

sections.h2: What is the Monroe County delinquent tax sale?
sections.html:
Right after April 15 the clerk issues a certificate of delinquency, a lien of record against the property. According to the clerk, that happens on or about April 16. Interest climbs monthly, so an early payment costs less.

The clerk scheduled the 2026 sale for September 23, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. Central, inside the clerk's office, and that date is behind us. A certificate unpaid at the sale may go to a private party who adds heavy administrative costs. The county attorney or a buyer may pursue foreclosure.

  • By mail: money orders only.
  • In person at the clerk's desk: check, cash or credit card, and card fees may apply.
  • Installments: the County Attorney's office offers them, though a sold bill no longer qualifies.

The clerk's page gives a phone number for learning whether a certificate was bought and by whom.

sections.h2: When are regular Monroe County bills due?
sections.html:
Through April 15 you pay the sheriff under the calendar in KRS 134.015. Fall brings the mailed bill, a 2 percent discount holds until November 1, and the printed amount can be paid up to December 31.

January costs an extra 5 percent, and later payments carry 10 percent. The state's property page gives a combined 21 percent penalty for February 1 through April 15. In its example a $1,000 bill becomes a $1,254 certificate, then totals $1,387.79 if the owner pays within five business days of the transfer.

sections.h2: How do you challenge a Monroe County value?
sections.html:
A PVA conference comes first, and the state requires it before anyone can file. The roll opens to the public on the first Monday of May for about two weeks, and the clerk's office accepts filings through the next workday after it closes.

The filing states your own opinion of value. Should bills go out before the appeal ends and the final figure beat your claim, a supplemental bill covers the gap. The board meets between 25 and 35 days after the window and may sit five days. Bring what the Department of Revenue lists as evidence: land and building details, insurance policies, construction costs and sales listings.

sections.h2: How are rural parcels valued in Monroe County?
sections.html:
Across 329 square miles and 34.4 people per square mile, many Monroe County sales come with land. The PVA must visit every parcel at least every four years and add new construction yearly, the Department of Revenue says. Farm land may be assessed at agricultural value instead of fair cash value, so ask the PVA how your acreage is classified before you list it.

Parcels near the Tennessee line, along the river or up in the hills can differ widely. If the roll shows a building that was torn down, or misses a barn you added, raise it at a PVA conference.

sections.h2: How does the homestead exemption work in Monroe County?
sections.html:
Anyone who owns and lives in a house and has turned 65, or carries a total disability classification, may claim it. Apply at the Monroe County PVA with proof, on the state's form.

KRS 132.810 sets one exemption per unit, even if the owner is both elderly and disabled, or several older residents share the unit. The amount follows a federal price index and is rechecked every two years. A sale or the owner's death must be reported to the PVA.

sections.h2: Can you sell a Monroe County house that owes tax?
sections.html:
Yes, and the usual route starts with a written payoff. The sheriff supplies it before April 15, and the clerk does afterward, when the figure rises monthly and carries the clerk and attorney fees.

Under KRS 134.015 the person who owned on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, and a lien can follow the property for 11 years. Houses in Monroe County that need work, or came to heirs, can change hands with a bill still open, so build the payoff into your numbers when you compare a listing with a cash sale.

faqs.q: Who accepts Monroe County property tax payments?
faqs.a: The county sheriff, in Suite E at 200 North Main Street, Tompkinsville. Call (270) 487-6622.

faqs.q: When did the 2026 Monroe County tax sale take place?
faqs.a: The clerk set it for September 23, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. Central. Phone (270) 487-5471 to learn whether a certificate was sold.

faqs.q: Is an installment plan available on a late Monroe County bill?
faqs.a: Yes, through the County Attorney's office, provided the certificate was not sold at the tax sale.

faqs.q: Can a delinquent bill be paid to the clerk by check in the mail?
faqs.a: No, mailed payments must be money orders. Checks, cash and credit cards work only at the clerk's office.

faqs.q: Where is the Monroe County PVA?
faqs.a: Suite A, 200 North Main Street, Tompkinsville. The office phone is (270) 487-6401.
